articles.title: Konkona Sen Sharma Shares Dengue Recovery Update From Hospital Bed
articles.excerpt: The actor posted a hospital-bed photo on Instagram, told followers she is 'better now,' and was back at Lust Stories 3 promotions by Sunday.
articles.image_caption: Konkona Sen Sharma shared a dengue recovery update from her hospital bed.
articles.nri_angle: Dengue remains a seasonal risk for diaspora travellers visiting India during the monsoon months — a reminder from an unlikely public-health messenger.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Measles-exposed Amtrak traveler rode through six California counties
articles.excerpt: An unvaccinated passenger later hospitalized with measles traveled by train and bus through six counties Sept. 12–14; L.A. Union Station visitors from Saturday 8 a.m.–noon should monitor symptoms through Oct. 3.
articles.image_caption: A close-up shows the red, blotchy measles rash spread across a person’s neck and upper chest. California health officials are warning of measles exposure across six counties after an unvaccinated Amtrak passenger traveled through the state Sept. 12–14.
articles.nri_angle: With Diwali travel weeks away, California's Indian diaspora families — frequent Amtrak and air travelers — should check MMR vaccination status before heading to busy stations or traveling to India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: At 81, This Gurugram Grandmother Is Still Travelling, Working — and Fully Confident
articles.excerpt: A viral Instagram video by Gurgaon-based founder Mehar Toor shows her 81-year-old grandmother — a businesswoman fresh off an Alaska cruise — explaining her philosophy in one line: she feels fully confident she can go anywhere.
articles.image_caption: An 81-year-old Gurugram grandmother pictured with her granddaughter, startup founder Mehar Toor. The dadi, a businesswoman and avid traveller, recently returned from an Alaska cruise.
articles.nri_angle: For diaspora families who track their elders' health across time zones, this dadi flips the script — a gentle challenge to every family that has quietly decided what an 81-year-old can and cannot do.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Raise Your Sum Insured or Buy Riders? How Experts Say to Prioritise
articles.excerpt: A cheap super top-up can take family cover to Rs 1 crore for about Rs 4,500 a year - but riders like consumables cover and critical-illness protection still earn their place. Here is how to prioritise.
articles.image_caption: A hospital exterior. Experts say the ideal target is about ₹1 crore of total health cover, and a super top-up is usually the cheapest way to raise it.
articles.nri_angle: A live question for NRIs insuring aging parents in India: a super top-up is the cheapest way to bring an old Rs 5 lakh policy up to a realistic level.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: PFRDA Finalises NPS Swasthya: 25% Medical Withdrawal Cap, Health Cover Up to Rs 30 Lakh
articles.excerpt: The pension regulator's September 18 guidelines spell out how much NPS Swasthya subscribers can draw for healthcare, the mandatory four-tier family-floater insurance, and what happens if a renewal premium goes unpaid.
articles.nri_angle: India-domestic product; the natural diaspora audience is NRIs planning retirement in India, though NRI eligibility details were not spelled out in the guidelines' published summaries.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Irregular Periods, Acne, Hair Thinning: 5 Signs You May Have PMOS
articles.excerpt: A doctor explains the five patterns — from unpredictable cycles to hair thinning — that warrant medical evaluation, and which tests a doctor may recommend.
articles.image_caption: A woman holds a calendar marked with question marks over expected period dates. Unpredictable or missed periods are among the key signs of PMOS that doctors say warrant medical evaluation.
articles.nri_angle: PMOS affects an estimated 1 in 8 women and often goes undiagnosed for years — an awareness gap this explainer addresses for women and families in the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Very Hot Tea and Coffee Triple Esophageal Cancer Risk, Major Study Finds
articles.excerpt: An Oxford analysis of nearly one million adults found the risk comes from heat itself — not tea or coffee — and that letting a drink cool for a few minutes may prevent a meaningful share of cases.
articles.image_caption: A cup of black tea. A new study found drinking very hot tea and coffee can triple esophageal cancer risk.
articles.nri_angle: For chai-drinking households, the study's simple takeaway — let the cup cool a few minutes before sipping — fits naturally into daily routine.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Acharya Balkrishna Says Turmeric Milk Is Ayurveda’s Go-To Cold and Cough Remedy
articles.excerpt: The Patanjali chairman’s prescription for cold season: warm milk, turmeric and a pinch of black pepper — supportive care backed by real pharmacology, but not a cure.
articles.image_caption: Acharya Balkrishna. He describes turmeric milk as Ayurveda's traditional remedy for colds and coughs.
articles.nri_angle: Diaspora families heading into cold season get a practical Ayurvedic remedy from Acharya Balkrishna — warm turmeric milk — with honest caveats about what it can and cannot do.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Exercise Can Cut Breast Cancer Risk — Which Workouts Help Most
articles.excerpt: A 15,550-woman international study found a 20% lower breast cancer risk for women who walked briskly about 2.7 hours a week — even those with a family history or BRCA mutations — while lab research shows contracting muscles release factors that slow cancer cell growth.
articles.image_caption: Exercising outdoors. New research links regular physical activity to a lower risk of breast cancer.

sources.label: FORCE (Facing Our Risk of Cancer Empowered) – XRAY review: 'Risk of breast cancer lowered with exercise regardless of family history'
World Economic Forum – 'Just a little exercise can lower breast cancer risk'

articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin women, among whom breast cancer is the most common cancer and genetic-screening conversations often lag, face a practical bar: about 30 minutes of brisk walking most days, with the biggest payoff for those with a family history who should also pursue regular screening.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Katrina Kaif on Postpartum Skin, Beauty Standards and Feeling Her Best
articles.excerpt: After facing trolling over her postpartum appearance, the actor says motherhood rebuilt her approach to skincare — and to what beauty means.
articles.image_caption: Katrina Kaif at a recent appearance. The actor has spoken about postpartum body image after facing online trolling.
articles.nri_angle: The postpartum body-shaming debate resonates with diaspora mothers navigating the same pressures across cultures — where family scrutiny can be as sharp as social media's.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Peter Chan Brought a Chengdu Dementia Care Home's Motto to Toronto
articles.excerpt: The veteran filmmaker drew on guidance from a Chengdu Alzheimer's care facility — "go with the flow, know when to stop" — while directing his early-onset dementia drama, starring Zhou Xun, which premieres at TIFF on September 18.
articles.image_caption: A film still from ‘The Road Not Taken’ shows the central family sharing a meal around a dinner table at night, the warm-lit scene viewed through a doorway. The Peter Chan-directed drama stars Zhou Xun as a television host confronting early-onset Alzheimer’s and premieres at the Toronto International Film Festival on September 18, 2026.
articles.nri_angle: In diaspora families where dementia is often handled privately with correction as the default, the Chengdu care home's counsel — don't argue with a drifting mind, and know when to let go — names a tension many caregivers of aging immigrant parents live with daily.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India bars stem cell therapy for autism as routine care
articles.excerpt: The health ministry's September 16 advisory says any stem cell use for autism must remain confined to duly approved clinical trials, following a January 2026 Supreme Court order; unauthorized treatment can now mean professional misconduct charges.
articles.image_caption: A clinical research laboratory shown in the reporting on the health ministry advisory. The September 16 advisory bars stem cell therapy for autism as routine care, restricting it to duly approved clinical trials under the ICMR-DBT 2017 guidelines.
articles.nri_angle: NRI parents exploring stem-cell clinics in India for autistic children now face a clear rule: commercial treatment is barred, and legitimate access runs only through approved clinical trials.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: From Navratri to Diwali: Dermatologists' Dos and Don'ts for Festive Skin
articles.excerpt: Nine nights of Garba, late-night parties and weeks of heavy makeup take a toll — dermatologists say the festive glow comes down to preparation, non-comedogenic makeup and double cleansing, not last-minute miracles.
articles.nri_angle: Whether you're doing Garba in New Jersey or Diwali in Dallas, the dermatologists' advice travels: the glow is built in the weeks before the first diya, not the morning of.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Turmeric Co. Takes Turmeric Shots to UK Clinics to Fight 'Pain Pandemic'
articles.excerpt: The functional-shot brand founded by ex-footballer Thomas Robson-Kanu is partnering healthcare practitioners across the UK to reach patients needing preventive solutions for inflammation and pain — putting Ayurveda's best-known root at the centre of a mainstream healthcare conversation.
articles.nri_angle: For South Asian consumers in the UK who grew up on haldi doodh, The Turmeric Co.'s clinic push is Ayurveda's most familiar ingredient going mainstream through a healthcare front door.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A 50-Millisecond Sound Burst Can Help Your Brain Wash Itself at Night
articles.excerpt: MIT researchers found that playing tiny bursts of pink noise at the precise peak of deep-sleep brain waves strengthens the flow of cerebrospinal fluid that clears metabolic waste — a discovery published in Science Translational Medicine with implications for Alzheimer's research.
articles.nri_angle: For households already debating white-noise machines and sleep trackers, the study suggests the future of sleep technology may be about timing — not volume.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Heart Surgeon Warns Smoking, Vaping Damage the Body 'From Top to Toes'
articles.excerpt: Board-certified cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Jeremy London says smoking in any form — tobacco, marijuana or vaping — is "the single worst thing you can do for your entire body," urging smokers to get help and those around them to offer support.
articles.image_caption: A metal ashtray filled with extinguished cigarette butts. Heart surgeon Dr Jeremy London warns that smoking and vaping in any form is the single worst thing for the body, damaging blood vessels and organs from the top of the head to the tip of the toes.
articles.nri_angle: South Asian diaspora tobacco use spans hookah, bidis and smokeless forms often left out of smoking conversations; Dr London's all-inhaled-forms warning and vaping alarm speak directly to those blind spots.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ayurveda Expert Shares 21-Day Routine for Glowing Skin, Centered on Gut Health
articles.excerpt: Dr Hansa Yogendra, director of The Yoga Institute in Mumbai, has laid out a three-week regimen built around a simple ginger-cardamom morning drink, gentle Ayurvedic skincare rituals and diet — arguing that radiant skin starts with a healthy gut.
articles.image_caption: Dr Hansa Yogendra, director of The Yoga Institute in Mumbai, who outlined the 21-day routine for glowing skin.
articles.nri_angle: The routine's ingredients — ginger, cardamom, turmeric, besan, rose water — are staples in most Indian diaspora kitchens, making this an accessible, culturally familiar wellness practice rather than a product to buy.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sepsis Kills 11 Million a Year. Handwashing and Vaccines Can Stop It
articles.excerpt: World Sepsis Day put the spotlight on a condition behind one in five global deaths — and the simple prevention steps experts say too many people skip.
articles.nri_angle: With India recording 11.3 million sepsis cases and 2.9 million deaths in 2020, diaspora families with elderly relatives or newborns — at home or visiting India — have the most to gain from hand hygiene, vaccination and knowing the warning signs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: PCOS Is Now PMOS: Doctors Say the New Name Changes Women's Care
articles.excerpt: The hormonal condition long known as polycystic ovary syndrome has been renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome — a change doctors say should push care beyond period regulation toward metabolic and mental health.
articles.nri_angle: For Indian-origin families who know the condition as PCOD, the PMOS rename reframes it as the whole-body metabolic and mental-health condition it is — with South Asian women's elevated diabetes and heart-disease risk making that reframing especially consequential.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Gold Imports Plunge 57% as Festive Season Tests India's Golden Appetite
articles.excerpt: August gold imports fell to $2.3 billion from $5.4 billion a year ago — and jewellers say the festive season will reshape, not erase, India's gold habit.
articles.image_caption: Gold jewellery on display at a shop in India. Gold imports fell 57% in August even as the festive and wedding season approaches.

sources.label: The Hindu BusinessLine (industry on Modi's gold appeal)
Reuters (jeweller stocks slide after Modi appeal)
Nation Press (trade data, gold import drop)

articles.nri_angle: Diaspora families planning weddings and festival-season gold purchases — in India or abroad — face the same price and policy crosswinds, and many watch the rupee and import-duty signals before buying.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
